spans.assertion: the analysis tested the hypothesis that referees are more likely to give red cards to dark-skinned than light-skinned players, using player-referee dyad data from European soccer leagues, 2012-2013 season

the analysis used linear probability models and logistic regression with cluster-robust standard errors to estimate adjusted risk differences and odds ratios, controlling for position, league, exposure, and referee country bias
the hypothesis is NOT SUPPORTED
the point estimate is a 0.21 percentage point higher probability of a red card for dark-skinned players (95% CI -0.08 to 0.50, p=0.153), not significant at α=0.05
the confidence interval includes zero and the effect is below the minimum detectable effect for this sample size
the adjusted risk difference (dark vs light skin) is 0.21 percentage points (0.002121 probability scale), 95% CI [-0.08, 0.50] pp, two-sided p=0.153

dark-skinned players have an estimated 0.21 pp higher probability of a red card than light-skinned players after adjusting for position, league, exposure, player characteristics, and referee country bias
the difference is not statistically significant and the CI spans negative, zero, and positive values
the adjusted odds ratio (dark vs light skin) is 1.20, 95% CI [0.96, 1.50], two-sided p=0.118
the odds of a red card are 1.20 times higher for dark-skinned players after adjustment
the result is not statistically significant and the CI includes 1.0
the unit of analysis is player-referee dyads, N=92,954 after excluding missing data
the dyad-level unit of analysis is not the same as individual match-level data
the original dataset had 146,028 dyads (2,053 players × 3,147 referees)
two independent raters coded player skin tone on a 0-1 scale (0=very light, 1=very dark)
the average of the two raters was used as the final skin tone measure
dark skin was defined as average ≥0.75 (10,411 dyads, 114 unique players)
light skin was defined as average ≤0.25 (90,116 dyads, 1,015 unique players)
medium skin tones (0.25-0.75) were excluded from analysis for clearer contrast
the final analysis sample was 92,954 dyads (83,582 light, 9,372 dark)
dyads were excluded for missing position (7%), height (<0.1%), weight (0.6%), or bias measures (0.1%)
the final sample represents 1,129 unique players and 2,730 unique referees
the outcome was operationalized as a binary indicator of any red card received in the dyad
red card rates were 1.22% for light skin (1,016/83,582), 1.41% for dark skin (132/9,372), and ~1.2% overall
the model controlled for player position (12 categories)
red card rates vary by position, highest for Center Backs (~2%), lowest for Right Midfielders (~0.7%)
dark-skinned players are more likely to play Center Forward/striker positions
the model controlled for league country (England, France, Germany, Spain)
dark-skinned player prevalence varies greatly by league (England/France ~15-23% dark vs Germany/Spain ~5% dark)
league is confounded with the referee bias measures
the model controlled for log(number of games) in the player-referee dyad
a log transformation of games was used because the distribution was right-skewed (median=1, max=47)
the model controlled for player height and weight
the model controlled for the number of yellow cards in the dyad
the model controlled for referee country implicit bias (meanIAT)
the model controlled for referee country explicit bias (meanExp)
a linear probability model estimated via OLS was used, with a binary (0/1) outcome
cluster-robust (Huber-White sandwich) standard errors were used
standard errors were clustered at the player level to address non-independence of dyads sharing a player
a secondary logistic regression analysis with cluster-robust SE was run
the secondary model used the same covariates and clustering as the primary model
24,094 medium-skin-tone dyads were excluded to create clearer contrast
complete-case analysis was used, excluding 7,573 dyads (7.5%) missing covariates
missing covariates broke down as: position 6,996 dyads, height 35, weight 590, bias measures 103
skin tone was averaged across raters then categorized (≤0.25 light, ≥0.75 dark)
games received a natural log transformation because the distribution was highly right-skewed
red cards were dichotomized to any vs none, from an original count variable of 0, 1, or 2
categorical variables were dummy-coded with the first category as reference

spans.note: intro sentence and table scaffolding for sensitivity table

spans.assertion: the full model gave 0.21 pp [-0.08, 0.50], p=0.153
the model without bias measures gave 0.20 pp [-0.09, 0.49], p=0.178
the minimal model (position + games only) gave 0.23 pp [-0.05, 0.51], p=0.108
results are robust to model specification
point estimates remain ~0.20-0.23 pp across all models, none statistically significant
the hypothesis is NOT SUPPORTED by the data
both the risk difference (p=0.153) and odds ratio (p=0.118) fail to reach significance at α=0.05, so the null cannot be rejected
the 95% CI for the risk difference [-0.08, 0.50] includes zero, consistent with no association as well as small positive or negative associations
the observed effect (0.21 pp) is only 57% of the minimum detectable effect (0.34 pp) at 80% power, so the study is underpowered
stratified-by-league analyses show heterogeneity: Germany +0.82 pp, England +0.27 pp, France -0.49 pp (dark vs light)
the data aggregate all matches within a player-referee pair
the analysis cannot distinguish whether red cards occurred in the first match vs after repeated encounters

spans.note: exposure controlled for but aggregation may dilute real effects

spans.assertion: skin tone was assessed from profile photos, not in-person observation
no formal inter-rater reliability assessment was reported for the two raters

spans.note: photos may vary in lighting, quality, age

spans.assertion: a 5-point skin-tone scale was collapsed to 2 categories (dark vs light), losing granularity
14.7% of skin tone data was missing (no photo available) and those players were excluded
the red card outcome was aggregated to binary (any vs none) rather than a count
dichotomizing loses information about multiple red cards (25 dyads had 2 red cards)
the analysis cannot distinguish a direct red card from a red card via two yellow cards
measurement error in skin tone likely biases estimates toward the null (non-differential misclassification)

spans.note: missing data could introduce selection bias if systematic

spans.assertion: player aggression/temperament, match importance/stakes, home/away status, score differential, and opponent characteristics were not measured or controlled for
dark-skinned players disproportionately play certain positions (forwards)

spans.note: position may be on the causal pathway if discrimination affects assignment
controlling for position might be over-adjustment

spans.assertion: no information is available on how referees were assigned to matches

spans.note: non-random assignment related to race could introduce bias

spans.assertion: the analysis cannot make strong causal claims

spans.note: associations may be confounded by unmeasured factors

spans.assertion: the study is underpowered; the minimum detectable effect (0.34 pp) is nearly 2x the observed effect (0.19 pp)
wide confidence intervals reflect high uncertainty
the dark-skinned player sample is relatively small (114 unique players vs 1,015 light-skinned)

spans.note: a true small effect could exist but be undetectable; absence of evidence is not evidence of absence

spans.assertion: the data are limited to the 2012-2013 season, four European leagues (England, France, Germany, Spain), and male professional soccer

spans.note: findings may not generalize to other periods, leagues, or sports

spans.assertion: numerous stratified and sensitivity analyses were conducted
no formal adjustment for multiple testing was applied

spans.note: risk of false positives in subgroups
league heterogeneity could be due to chance

spans.assertion: implicit and explicit bias were measured at the country level, aggregated from online samples
individual referees' actual bias is unknown / not measured
country-level bias is conflated with league

spans.note: may reflect population differences rather than referee attitudes

spans.assertion: the analysis cannot test whether individual referee bias moderates skin tone effects

spans.note: country-level bias may be a poor proxy for referee decision-making

spans.assertion: the model assumed a linear relationship between covariates and probability
the linearity assumption was assessed as reasonable for binary covariates; continuous covariates may have nonlinear effects but likely minimal impact given small coefficients
the model assumed dyads are independent conditional on player-level clustering
player-level clustering was addressed via robust standard errors
potential residual clustering by referee was not addressed, which could understate uncertainty
the model assumed homoscedasticity (constant error variance)
homoscedasticity is not strictly met with a binary outcome, but cluster-robust SE addresses this

spans.note: generic LPM property: can predict outside [0,1]

spans.assertion: out-of-range predictions were assessed as not a concern here since the event rate is low (~1.2%) and all predicted probabilities fell within [0,1]
the complete-case analysis assumed data are MCAR or MAR conditional on observed covariates
missing position data (7%) is the most substantial source of missingness

spans.note: if missingness relates to unmeasured characteristics, estimates could be biased

spans.assertion: sensitivity analyses suggest the results are robust
the analysis assumed all important confounders were measured and included
the no-unmeasured-confounding assumption was assessed as likely violated because player aggression, match context, and referee assignment were not measured; direction of bias is unknown
by league, Germany shows the largest difference (+0.82 pp favoring light skin), while France and Spain show a reversed pattern (light skin higher red-card rate)
heterogeneity across leagues undermines the hypothesis of consistent discrimination
by position, defensive positions show +0.30 pp and offensive positions +0.11 pp, with the effect slightly larger for defenders
by exposure, the effect was +0.05 pp at 1 game, +0.50 pp at 2-3 games, +0.39 pp at 4-10 games, and +0.19 pp at 11+ games
there is no clear dose-response pattern by exposure

the strongest significant predictors in the full model were log(games) +1.29 pp (p<0.001), Center Back +1.26 pp (p<0.001), yellow cards +0.45 pp (p<0.001), Goalkeeper +0.82 pp (p<0.001), and France league +0.53 pp vs England (p=0.005)
the skin tone (darkSkin) coefficient was not among the statistically significant predictors
the analysis found no statistically significant evidence that dark-skinned players receive more red cards, after adjustment

point estimates consistently suggest a small positive association (~0.2 pp), but it is not statistically significant (p=0.15), uncertain (CI includes zero and negative values), small relative to the minimum detectable effect (57%), and inconsistent across subgroups
the findings are most consistent with no true association, or an effect too small to reliably detect; the observed non-significant estimate is consistent with sampling variability around a true null
the hypothesis is NOT SUPPORTED
analyses were conducted in Python using statsmodels, pandas, numpy, and scipy
complete reproducible code is provided in final_analysis.py
the analysis used publicly available data (soccer.csv) with documented variable definitions (codebook.txt)
no data or results were fabricated; all reported findings were directly generated from the provided data using documented methods
standard errors and confidence intervals were calculated using cluster-robust methods as specified
all methodological decisions (variable definitions, exclusions, transformations, model specifications) are fully documented in the report
